about: Walichrum (the drowned trading place near Domburg on Walcheren), written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/walichrum.md and the spine. One port. A draft for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what the sources do not show; the dossier's section 8 lists what must not be claimed, and this file keeps to it: no toll house, mint, church or quay is recorded here, the place lay behind the dunes, and nobody alive in 793 knows the name of the goddess under the sand.

ports.summary: Walichrum is a long strip of oak houses behind the dunes of Walcheren, the king's ground, where Dorestad's trade meets the sea. In 793 its best coin years are behind it, but the marsh still gives salt, cheese, wool and hides, and ships for England wait here for a wind. A merchant comes for cheap salt in autumn, for news of the crossing, and to sell Rhine pots and oak to people who have neither clay nor trees.
ports.seasons: The sheep go out on the salt marsh after Easter and are shorn about Saint John's (a guess); cheese comes from the hay month on. The salt is boiled from Lammas, and by Michaelmas it is cheap, in time for the Martinmas slaughter. From Martinmas to Easter gales stand on the shoals, little moves, and the sea is looked at every morning from the high dune.

history.text: About this year Willibrord breaks an idol of the old belief at the villa Walichrum. Its keeper strikes him on the head with a sword and does not wound him, and dies three days later.
history.source: Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi (about 796), not quoted; the year is local tradition (zeeuwseankers.nl, Willibrord op Walcheren) (?)

history.text: The years of the small thick silver pennies: about a thousand of them will be picked off this beach a thousand years on. Whether any were struck here is not known.
history.source: Metcalf and Op den Velde 2009-10; a mint here for the first 'porcupine' pennies is a hypothesis only

history.text: About now the small thick pennies go out of use. The coin of the strand is the Frankish king's denier.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sceat; the dossier reckons them forty years out of use by 793

history.text: An oak is felled near Hamwic for an English clinker ship. Her planks end their days on this island.
history.source: Ufkes 2012, Paleo-aktueel 23 (tree-ring date of ship timber found in the ring fort)

history.text: About this year Alcuin writes the Life of Willibrord for Beornrad of Echternach, and names the villa Walichrum.
Frederick becomes bishop of Utrecht (815 or 816). He is said to have preached on the island and to have charged its people with marrying close kin.
history.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_of_Utrecht; the Passio Friderici as quoted at frisiacoasttrail.blog (a later text) (?)

history.text: This year, a week before Saint John's, Northmen fell on our people unprepared on the island called Walacria, killed many and plundered more. They stayed some while, took what tribute they liked, and went on to Dorestad and did the same.

Eggihard, count of that place, and Hemming, Halfdan's son, a Dane in the emperor's service, are killed here on the same day. The heathen lead many women away captive. A star with a tail is seen that year.
history.source: Annales Fuldenses 837 and Thegan, as quoted at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemming_Halfdansson (Latin not opened); Annales Xantenses 837 (von Simson 1909), our rendering

history.text: The emperor gives up his journey to Rome and comes to Noviomagus. The inquiry lays the loss partly to impossibility and partly to the disobedience of some. Abbots and counts are sent to curb the Frisians, and a fleet is ordered.
On Saint Stephen's day the sea covers nearly all Frisia, almost to the tops of the dunes. Two thousand four hundred and thirty-seven are counted drowned.
history.source: Annales Bertiniani 839 (the annal's own count and its own word, dunos); chronicle_793.json 838-12-26-frisia-flood

history.text: About these years a ring fort of sods with a moat is begun by the dunes, the largest of five on the islands. Others date it after 851, or about 890. Who built it is not known.
history.source: Ufkes 2012 (835-838); ten Harkel and others 2023 (after 851); kzgw.nl (about 890) (?)

history.text: Lothar gives Walcheren and the places round it to the Dane Harald. The annalist calls it a deed to be detested, that Christians should serve men who worship demons.
Harald is dead by this year. His brother Rorik takes Dorestad and is given it by the same king.
About now the traders are gone from the strand. Inside the fort five byre-houses are farmed until about 950.
history.source: Ufkes 2012; ten Harkel and others 2023 has the beach used, more thinly, into the tenth century

history.text: Between this year and 892 great fleets pass the island eight times. The army winters at Ganda in 879.
About now blown sand drives the last people inland from the old strand.
Count Baldwin of Flanders is said to receive Walcheren in fief from the emperor.
On Michaelmas eve a sea flood wrecks the island.

eras.text: The long street behind the dunes, a little past its best. No wall, no church, no tower: houses, pens, pits and four grave fields. Ships for England and for the Rhine lie on the creek mud together. The king's steward is the only officer, and he is mostly counting sheep.

Quieter and warier. Bishop Frederick's priests come out from Traiectum and scold. Guard ships are talked of more than seen. From 834 every summer brings word of fleets on the Rhine, and the count sets a watch on the high dune.

After the raid. The count and the emperor's Dane are dead, many women are gone north, and tribute has been taken. Sods are being cut for a ring wall. On Saint Stephen's day 838 the sea comes almost over the dunes. Fewer ships; salt and wool still.

Harald's years. A heathen lord's hall on a Christian shore: no toll, but a gift in kind, and his men take what they like from those who bring none. The fleets that pass leave the strand alone. Priests stay away.
The last traders. Harald is dead and Rorik holds Dorestad. One house in three stands empty; the timbers of the rest are taken down and carried inland one by one. The ring fort has byres in it.
Farms inside the wall and a few on the old strand. Great fleets pass and nobody goes down to the water to look. Sand lies against the west doors.
The fort's farms are given up. The old street is posts in the sand, and after a gale the dead show in the dune foot. The people live inland, and churches are rising on the island.

After the flood of 1014 the island is the count of Flanders's and the churches of Saint Willibrord's. Where the trading place stood there is beach. Fishermen find pennies there and do not know whose face is on them.

sites.name: The creek strand
sites.see: A tidal creek behind the dunes, grey mud shining at the ebb, with ships sitting upright on it in a row: two broad Frisian hulls, an English one with a tall stem, flat Rhine barges. Men wade between them with sacks on their shoulders. Behind, the dune line and a wide pale sky; gulls, the suck of mud, the smell of weed and tar.
sites.source: Where boats lay is not known: the creek is an assumption (dossier 1; one account joins the place to the Scheldt by a creek, frisiacoasttrail.blog (?)). The tide of about 3.3 m is the project's estimate (Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md). The pilot met here is the spine's cast.gerlef, whose home is Witla.

sites.name: The long street
sites.see: A sandy way running east and west between oak houses with upright plank walls, a thousand paces and more, never straight. Goods lie on hides in front of doors: grey Rhine pots, querns, cheeses, fleeces, a tray of glass beads. Dung heaps and stock pens stand between the houses; pigs root for acorns. It smells of sheep and peat smoke.
sites.source: de Man 1899 (Frederiks's strip of about 1,300 m; 'a sort of street' running east-west in tradition, irregular family groups as he saw them; dung heaps, pens, acorns); ten Harkel and others 2023 (Rhenish pottery, querns, glass). What the market looked like is not known (?)

sites.name: The brooch-maker's hearth
sites.see: A lean-to against a house wall: a pit hearth lined with stones and red clay, bellows of sheepskin, clay moulds drying on a plank. A man sits cross-legged filing the edge of a small bronze brooch. Green sparks when he blows the fire; the sharp smell of hot copper.
sites.source: ten Harkel and others 2023 (brooch-making in copper alloy); de Man 1899 (hearth pits lined with stones and red clay)

sites.name: The tan pits
sites.see: Square pits dug at the marsh edge, full of brown water with hides sunk under hurdles. Ox horns lie in a heap, and strips of trimmed leather hang on a rail. A boy stirs with a pole. The stink reaches the street on a south wind; nobody builds downwind.
sites.source: de Man 1899 (tanning pits with leather strips and ox horns)

sites.name: The salt hearths
sites.see: Out on the marsh, low mounds of ash and a row of clay hearths under a reed roof with no walls. Men dig the salt-soaked ground, burn it, wash the ash and boil the brine in clay pans. White smoke lies flat on the grass; sacks stand ready on a sledge. The air tastes of salt and peat.
sites.source: kzgw.nl, Vikings in Walcheren (salt boiled from salt-soaked soil); the autumn season is the project's guess (Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md 2.3); works_793.json salt_pan

sites.name: The sheep marsh
sites.see: Flat green salt marsh cut by silver creeks as far as can be seen, dotted with sheep. A woman sits milking a ewe at a hurdle pen; cheeses dry on a rack under a net against the gulls. Larks, wind, the bleat of lambs, and the sea heard but not seen.
sites.source: ten Harkel and others 2023 (sheep farmers on salt marsh, eating mostly from the land; wool and cloth tied to the abbeys of Ghent and Echternach); works_793.json flock_share

sites.name: Wiltrud's house
sites.see: A house like the others, ten paces by fourteen, with one middle room and a fire on the earth floor. Benches along the plank walls, a cask on trestles, cups of green glass on a shelf beside wooden ones. Skippers of three tongues sit apart and listen to each other. Smoke, wet wool and sour ale.
sites.source: de Man 1899 (houses of 5-10 by 14 m, a central room with side rooms, earth floors; glass cups, one of them green and footless). The ale-house itself is invented

sites.name: The king's house
sites.see: The longest house on the street, squared oak trunks at its corners, with a fenced yard, a tally shed and a pen of the king's sheep. A spear leans by the door. Inside, a high seat with a carved back and a bench for those who wait. From 841 a Danish shield hangs over the door.
sites.source: A royal estate from the late sixth century is Erfgoed Zeeland's reading, not a charter (?); the first named count is Eggihard, killed 837 (Annales Fuldenses); Harald from 841 (Annales Bertiniani). No reeve, toll or court is recorded here: the house and its uses are the game's

sites.name: Where the idol stood
sites.see: A bare place at the west end of the street where nothing is built: a pit grown over with grass and a plain oak cross, grey with weather, taller than a man. Mussel shells and a twist of wool lie at its foot. Sheep graze up to it and no closer. Wind in the marram grass.
sites.source: Alcuin, Vita Willibrordi: an idol stood at Walichrum and Willibrord broke it. The cross, the place in the street and the things left at its foot are invented (?). No church or priest is recorded here in 793; a priest out of Traiectum saying Mass in the open at the great feasts is the game's. Churchmen thought the islanders half heathen (Thiofrid, about 1103; the Passio Friderici)

sites.name: The fenced graves
sites.see: A long grave field between the houses and the dune, fenced with oak pales, three hundred paces by seventy. On the west a gate of two great tree trunks. Inside, low mounds in rows, all lying the same way, heads to the west. A new coffin waits on trestles: a hollowed trunk with a thin lid.
sites.source: de Man 1899 (Westhove: about 50 graves, 7th to 9th century, fenced with oak pales, 325 paces by 70, a gate of two great trunks on the west; trunk coffins pegged with wood, a small board under the head, heads to the west); ten Harkel and others 2023 (four grave fields; churchyard burial on this coast only from the tenth century)

sites.name: The menders' bank
sites.see: The firm bank at the head of the creek, where a barge lies on rollers with three strakes off. Old planks are stacked by length under a hide; a man splits an oak log with wedges, another boils tar in a pot. Nothing here is thrown away. Axe strokes, and the smell of pitch.
sites.source: ten Harkel and others 2023 and Ufkes 2012 (planks of an English clinker ship and of Rhine barges reused on the island, some as coffins; oak hewn with the axe). The yard is invented: the island has no timber, which is why oak is wanted (goods_793.json)

sites.name: The high dune
sites.see: The tallest dune, with a path worn up its landward side. From the top: the whole long street below, the marsh and its creeks behind, and to seaward white water on the shoals off the north-west corner. A boy lies in the grass watching for sails. No tower, no stone, no mark but the dune itself.
sites.source: de Man 1899 (no tower or stone building); Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md (the Banjaard shoals off the north-west corner). The watch is invented; the place lay behind the dunes (kzgw.nl)

sites.name: The ring wall
sites.see: A round bank of stacked sods as high as two men, a wet ditch outside it, two roads crossing in the middle and four gaps for gates. Inside there is room for every beast on the island. Long byre-houses stand in the quarters, and cattle look out of the doors.
sites.source: Ufkes 2012 (sod rampart and moat, 4.5 ha, two crossing roads, five byre-houses of about 875-950, begun 835-838 on his dating); others date it after 851 or about 890, and its builders are unknown (zeeuwseankers.nl, Ringforts) (?)

people.name: Wiltrud
people.trait: Remembers what every skipper drank, owed and said, and in what order.
people.want: Her daughter married off the island, to a man with a ship and all his teeth.
people.fear: A winter when no hull comes, and the day her own name is the news.
people.voice: Dry and short. Says the price first and the welcome after. Never asks a question she cannot already answer.
people.looks: About forty, broad, red hands, a grey wool dress pinned at the shoulder with a small bronze brooch, a ring of keys and an ear-scoop on her belt, a green glass cup in her fist.
knows: who lies on the strand and where she is bound
what salt, cheese and wool fetch here this week
which skipper is hiring and which is not paying
what was said last by a ship from England
who on the island still keeps old pennies in a pot

ties.note: her brother; she sold his first brooch for him and took a third
buys her cheese and carries her news out to the marsh
he wants a count kept of her casks; she wants him to pay for what he drinks
the pilot sleeps by her fire when he works this mouth, and pays in news
he stood her a cask of Rhine wine one hungry spring and has not let her forget it
skippers tell her what they did not tell him
the ale-wife at the fort on the Scheldt; skippers carry each one's opinion of the other's brewing
the ale-wife at Ganda: salt goes up the river, smoked eels come down, and the news with both
an English ale-wife who says the island's ale would need to be strong
sends her salt up the Seine each autumn with a message scratched on the sack

lines.greet: Ale is a penny for four cups. Sit where you can see the door. You are from the river, by the boat.
lines.greet_again: You again. The same bench, and the same cup. You left owing nothing, which I remember.
rumour: An English keel came in on Tuesday's tide, sailing light. Turned away somewhere. Her master drinks and does not say where.
Salt will be cheap by Michaelmas and cheaper by Martinmas. Buy it when the smoke lies flat on the marsh.
The king's man counted the sheep twice this spring. Somebody upriver wants wool, or wants to know who has it.
lines.saying: A guest who pays is kin. A kinsman who does not is a guest.
lines.to_heir: You have your father's way of looking at the cask before the company. He sat there. Sit.
lines.farewell: Go with the ebb, keep off the north-west corner, and bring me back what they are saying in Lundenwic.

people.source: invented; Wil- and -trud are Frisian name parts (Design/content/peoples/frisian.md 7; Wil- as in Willibrord (?)). The keys, ear-scoop and green glass cup are grave and beach finds (de Man 1899; kzgw.nl)

people.name: Reginbert
people.trait: A Frank set over an island of Frisians, who counts the king's sheep because he cannot count on the islanders.
people.want: A full tally at Michaelmas, and to be called back to the mainland before he dies.
people.fear: A missus of the king asking why so little comes off so much marsh.
people.voice: Proud and exact. Names the king in every third sentence. Speaks to islanders slowly, as if to the deaf.
people.looks: Past forty, lean, clean-shaven with a long moustache, a blue cloak to the knee, a bundle of notched tally sticks on a thong and a short sword he has never drawn.
knows: what is the king's on this island and what is not
what the abbeys of Ganda and Echternach take from their land by the Scheldt mouth
the king's new penny and the fine for refusing it
when a king's man last looked into hulls here
the road to the palace at Noviomagus and who has the count's ear there

ties.note: sends his tallies up the river to the count's court; has met him twice
the two stewards write to each other about measures and complain about Frisians
he would like to count her casks; he drinks there all the same
the king's ewes run with hers, and her count of the lambs is always right
the abbey's man takes wool from ground Reginbert thinks is the king's
the palace clerk takes his tallies and mends his Latin
an order about English ships came down the coast under the abbot's name; he read it aloud and nobody listened
the toll man on the Scheldt, the nearest officer he can ask for an account, and does
the wright at Ganda owes him for a raft of oak that came round by the island

lines.greet: This is the king's ground. Trade on it freely and honestly. Whose man are you, and what is under that hide?
lines.greet_again: The Dorestad boat. Good. You at least know what a measure is.
rumour: The lord king has made his penny heavier, and it must be taken in every place and market. Tell that to an islander with a pot of old ones.
The king keeps Easter at a palace and the counts go to him. If you want a thing from a count, be at Noviomagus when the feast is.
I asked how many live on this strand. They said: enough. I have been here nine years.
lines.saying: They count sheep by the leg here and divide by four. It is the only sum on which the island and I agree.
lines.to_heir: Your father dealt straight with me. On this island that is rare enough to write down, and I did.
lines.farewell: Go in the king's peace. And if they ask upriver, say Reginbert's tallies are in order.

people.source: invented. No reeve or steward is recorded at Walichrum; a royal estate here is a modern reading (Erfgoed Zeeland 2018) (?). The steward of a royal estate is the iudex of the Capitulare de villis; the new denier is Frankfurt 794 c. 5 (chronicle_793.json)

people.name: Wilbraht
people.trait: A brooch-maker with quick hands and a family story he does not tell: his great-grandfather kept the idol.
people.want: Good bronze, tin he can trust, and his work worn in places he will never see.
people.fear: Priests who ask about his kin; a buyer who bites the metal.
people.voice: Talks to the work, not the customer. Answers a hard question with a harder one, or a riddle.
people.looks: Under thirty, slight, burn scars on both forearms, hair tied back with a thong, a leather apron, tweezers and a file on a cord round his neck.
knows: what bronze, tin and old silver are worth by weight
the old small pennies, and which of them are good silver
what English and Danish women are wearing this year, from what skippers ask for
what his grandmother said happened at the idol
riddles, of the kind with two answers

ties.note: his elder sister; she sells for him and takes a third
she knows whose great-grandson he is and has never said it to a priest
the moneyer melts what Wilbraht would rather keep and look at
an old thing, and all on Wilbraht's side: Saint Martin's house holds the story that shames his kin
they trade riddles; Ravn has not yet lost one to him
a Dane who sends him moulds to copy and gets brooches back by any ship going north
the comb-maker on the Scheldt; they winter at the same hearth and swap rivets for tin
a craftswoman over the water who calls his brooches Frisian tin; he has seen hers
buys his broken beakers for the melt, by way of the goldsmith Soti

lines.greet: Do not stand in the light. If you want a brooch, say for whom. If you want old silver weighed, say how much.
lines.greet_again: The pin held, then. They do. Sit down, I am pouring, and it will not wait.
rumour: A woman in Ripa wants them round, a woman in Lundenwic wants them like a cross. I make both from the same pot.
They still turn up the small thick pennies with a spade here. The king will not take them. The Danes will, on a scale.
A monk was asking the old people what they saw at the west end. They saw nothing. They were not born.
lines.saying: I have one tooth and bite two cloaks together. Say what I am.
lines.to_heir: Your father carried my work north and brought back the price. You have his hands. Are they as honest?
lines.farewell: Keep it dry and it will outlast you. Most things I make do.

people.source: invented; brooch-making in copper alloy at Domburg is ten Harkel and others 2023; tweezers are a beach find (kzgw.nl). The keeper of the idol is in Alcuin; that he left kin is the game's (?). The riddle (a brooch pin) is ours, in the Exeter manner

people.name: Bernhild
people.trait: Runs sixty ewes on the marsh, makes the best cheese on the island, and has nursed her sister for eleven years without a word about it.
people.want: Linen, honey and anything that eases her sister Thiadwih's face; a fair price for wool.
people.fear: That she dies first, and nobody will go into the side room.
people.voice: Plain and slow. Says a thing once. Blesses herself, and then touches wood as well.
people.looks: Forty-five, tall, weathered, a brown dress with two pins and a string of glass beads between them, a hairpin of bone, a shepherd's crook, a cheese cloth over her arm.
knows: wool, fleeces and cheese: what they weigh and what they fetch
what the abbeys' men pay for marsh wool, and when they come
the weather from the sheep and the sky
who lies in which grave field, and with what laid on their shoulder
what her grandmother told of the day the idol was broken

ties.note: sells her cheese and hears the strand's news from her
herds the king's ewes with her own, on halves
keeps his family's secret; he made her beads into a string for nothing
her grandson, born in 803; she will not live to see him at the salt hearths
the abbey's man advanced her silver on next year's wool in the hungry spring
a wise woman of the east coast once sent her a salve by a skipper, and the making of it by word of mouth

lines.greet: You want wool or cheese. The wool is shorn at Saint John's. The cheese is there. Mind the dog.
lines.greet_again: You came back, and by the marsh path, not the street. Then you came to see me. Sit.
rumour: The sheep lay facing the land this morning. Do not sail tomorrow.
The abbey's man from Ganda pays in silver before the shearing and counts fleeces after. He has never once counted short in my favour.
My grandmother saw the bishop struck with a sword and not bleed. She said the sword was blunt. She said it quietly.
lines.saying: Bury a man with a penny on his shoulder. Whoever asks for it there will be told he has paid.
lines.to_heir: Your father brought honey for my sister when he had no need to. Take a cheese. No. Take it.
lines.farewell: God keep you, and the wood of your boat.

people.source: invented; Bern- and -hild are Frisian name parts (Design/content/peoples/frisian.md 7). A disfigured woman nursed for years is ten Harkel and others 2023; women's beads, keys and hairpins, and coins laid on the right shoulder of the dead, are de Man 1899

people.name: Unno
people.trait: Bernhild's grandson: boils salt, speaks for the strand when somebody must, and has outlived two lords of it.
people.want: His sister Berntrud back from the north; the pans left alone by whoever holds the hall.
people.fear: Sails in June. A high tide with a north-west wind behind it.
people.voice: A dry Frisian who says the worst thing first and plainly, then offers you salt at a fair price.
people.looks: Thirties, short and thick, grey ash to the elbows, a hooded wool cape cut short at the hip, a wooden salt rake, eyes red from the smoke.
knows: salt: when it is cheap, who is buying, what it fetches in the north
who was taken in the year of the raid, and to which market they are said to have gone
what Harald's men want as a gift, and what offends them
where the high ground is when the sea comes in
what your house did here in his grandmother's day

ties.note: his grandmother; he keeps her flock mark and her way of saying a thing once
kept the count's dune watch, and was on the marsh the morning it mattered
the Dane bought his salt and learned his children's names
brings the strand's gift to the hall each autumn and speaks as little as he can
from 850 they send salt and word between the island and Dorestad

the bishop's canon preached at the cross that the islanders are half heathen and marry their kin (the charge is the Passio Friderici's; that Odulf carried it here is the game's (?)); Unno was standing in front
the bishop whose canons call the islanders half heathen; the island has stopped sending to him
sells her salt for salt pork, and sends word up with the salt when sails are seen
the abbey's steward, who buys the island's salt on credit until the wool silver comes in

lines.greet: Salt is three pennies the sack at the hearth, less after Michaelmas. Your house bought from my grandmother. I know the boat.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat. Good. I have kept ten sacks dry for you, and a thing to ask.
rumour: Witla burned last summer, and the town on the Scheldt. We are the next strand down the coast. The count says ships are promised.
They came a week before Saint John's, on the morning tide. The count is dead, and the Dane with him. My sister is gone north.
The new lord takes no toll. He takes a gift. The difference is that you choose it, and he chooses whether it was enough.
lines.saying: The emperor's ships are like the Last Day: promised, certain, and not this year.
lines.to_heir: Your father stood with us when it was not his island. Salt at my price, for you, as long as I boil.
lines.farewell: Sail before the wind turns north-west. If you go by the Danes' markets, ask after a woman named Berntrud.

people.source: invented; Unno is an attested Frisian short name (Design/content/peoples/frisian.md 7). Salt-boilers: kzgw.nl. Witla and Antwerp burned in 836 (Annales Bertiniani; Annales Fuldenses); the raid and the women led away captive are Annales Bertiniani and Xantenses 837; the gift in kind under Harald is trade_year_793.json's note. The short cape is the Frisian cloak Notker's Franks mocked (Gesta Karoli I.34)

people.name: Eggihard
people.trait: The emperor's count on an island with no wall, in years when the emperor's sons are at war with their father.
people.want: Ships, a levy that comes when called, and one answer from the palace before the sailing season.
people.fear: Sails from the north on a morning tide, and islanders who will not leave their sheep to stand in a line; and the emperor's inquiry into who let the fleets through, which will want a name.
people.voice: A Frank, proud of his lord and short of patience. Gives orders as questions and does not wait for the answer.
people.looks: About forty, heavy in the shoulder, a cropped dark beard going grey, a faded red cloak pinned with a round enamelled brooch, a mail shirt he wears even to table, a horn at his hip.
knows: what the palace has promised and what has come
where fleets were seen last summer, from Dorestad to the Scheldt
who on the island will fight and who will hide
the law on arms: no mail or blades to strangers
what a merchant could carry upriver for him, and what it would be worth
how many keels went up the Maas and when, as far as the pilot at Witla has told him
which Frisians will turn out for the watch and which will pay the Northmen instead

ties.note: the Dane was sent to stiffen his guard; they did not expect to like each other
Unno serves him: the dune watch is Unno's kin, paid in the count's bread
the palace clerk reads his letters to those who decide, and has not yet had an answer to give him
the bishop's canon brings him more news than the palace does
sends word up the river to the king's men at Dorestad when a fleet has passed, for what it is worth by then; in his years the moneyer Sigibald is the one who is always there to hear it
trusts the Witla pilot's count of sails over his own men's
the king of the Danes sends word that the fleets are not his; the count buries the men they kill
the emperor Louis, who comes to Nijmegen each time too late (?)
counted spears at the fort on the Scheldt in the years before it burned; she fed his men
the abbey's wool passes the river mouth under his watch, and its steward remembers it

lines.greet: A Dorestad merchant. You came down the river: what did you see on it? Ships, I mean. Not yours.
lines.greet_again: You keep coming back to an island with no wall. Either trade is good or you are a brave man.
rumour: They burned Witla. They burned the town on the Scheldt. I have forty spears, an island of shepherds, and a letter from the palace.
The emperor ordered guard ships built when I was a boy. I would like to know which river they are on.
A blade sold to a Northman is a crime. I say it to every hull. Some of them look at the ballast when I do.
The emperor has ordered ships built. I have seen the order. I have not seen a ship.
The king of the Danes says these are not his men. Then he will not mind what I do when I catch one.
Antwerp has a fort and Witla has a pilot and a fire basket. Tell me which you would burn first.
lines.saying: The palace asks how many ships I saw. I answer. Then it asks again next year.
lines.farewell: If you go by Noviomagus, tell them what you saw here. Use small words.
lines.ask: If you sail up river, tell them at Dorestad what you saw here. They will not believe a count. They may believe a merchant.
lines.greet_witla: Merchant. How many sails did you see between here and the island, and standing which way? Think before you answer.
lines.farewell_witla: Go while the water is empty. If you see smoke behind you, do not come back to look.
lines.saying_witla: A watch that is kept by turns is kept by nobody.

people.source: Historical: Eggihard (Eccihard), count 'of that place', killed on Walcheren on 17 June 837 (Annales Fuldenses 837 and Thegan, as quoted at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemming_Halfdansson). Nothing else is known of him: the year he took office, his character and every word here are invented (?). Witla and Antwerp: Annales Bertiniani 836. The fleet ordered: chronicle_793.json 810-fleet-ordered-810. One person with the count whom the Witla file first wrote as its own (witla.eggihard, folded in here on 6 Oct 2026): that the watch at the Maas mouth was his and that he came to Witla in 834-836 is the game's (?), from realms/francia.json; his lines for Witla are kept as greet_witla, ask, saying_witla and farewell_witla. The inquiry and the order for ships are Annales Bertiniani 837

people.name: Hemming
people.trait: Halfdan's son: a Dane of high kin, baptised, in the emperor's service, set to guard a Christian shore against his own countrymen.
people.want: To be judged by what he does on this strand, not by where he was born.
people.fear: To see a sail he knows.
people.voice: A Dane: says less than he means, and the worst of it last and smallest. Polite to merchants, since he has been one's guest.
people.looks: Fifty or near it, tall, grey-fair hair worn long, a Frankish cloak over a Danish tunic, a silver cross on a cord worn outside the shirt, a broad axe at his belt.
knows: how a fleet chooses a shore: the tide, the wind, the hour
the names of the great men among the Danes and who is out of favour
what a captive fetches at the Danes' markets and how one is bought back
the Danish tongue, and what the islanders say when they think he cannot follow
that an island cannot be held with forty men

ties.note: stands with the count, and will on the last day
buys his salt and asks after his sister
of the same exiled house of the Danes, by the usual reckoning (?); they have chosen different lords
the king of the Danes is of the line that drove his kin out
a younger man of the same house (?), raiding where Hemming guards

lines.greet: You are the merchant from the river. I am the count's Dane. The islanders have another name for me. It is shorter.
lines.greet_again: You are back. The tide table in my head had you a day sooner.
rumour: They will come on a morning flood with the wind behind them. I would. It is not a hard thing to know.
If one of yours is taken, go north before winter with silver, not after. By spring they are sold on east.
I was baptised with water. The men who are coming will not ask to see it.
lines.saying: A guard dog is still a wolf's cousin. The sheep remember it, and so does the wolf.
lines.farewell: Fair wind. If you see many sails together, do not count them. Turn.

people.source: Historical: Hemming son of Halfdan, a Dane in Frankish service, called 'a most Christian leader' by Thegan, killed with Eggihard on 17 June 837 (Annales Fuldenses 837; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemming_Halfdansson). Whether he held the island in fief is not known, and his kinship to Harald and Rorik is a modern reconstruction (?). His age, character and words are invented

people.name: Harald
people.trait: A Danish exile of the royal kin, given the island by Lothar to keep other Danes off it: a heathen lord's peace on a Christian shore.
people.want: Gifts that show he is a lord and not a hired guard; a kingdom among the Danes if one comes loose.
people.fear: That Lothar finds a cheaper Dane; that his brother does better than he has.
people.voice: Slow, courteous, and listening for the insult. Speaks Frankish well and chooses not to. Takes a gift without thanks and remembers it for ever.
people.looks: Forty or more, broad, a red beard going grey, a fine Frankish cloak worn as plunder is worn, thick silver rings on both arms, a hammer on a cord at his neck.
knows: which fleets are out this summer and whose they are
what Lothar promised him and what Lothar's brothers think of it
what is sold at the Danes' markets and who sells it
who on this island gave freely and who had to be asked
where his brother Rorik is, most years

ties.note: his brother; they held Dorestad together under the old emperor, and Rorik will hold it again when Harald is dead
the king of the Danes sits where Harald's house sat
the salter brings the strand's gift and is the only islander who speaks to him without shaking
a kinsman (?) who died for the Franks on the ground Harald now holds from them
a young man of his hall who learns here how a Dane takes a Frankish king's dues
the abbey's wool land by the river mouth pays Harald now, and the abbey writes to kings about it
the ale-wife up the Scheldt, whose boats all pay him something first; she has said what she thinks of it

lines.greet: A merchant. Good. I take no toll here. A guest brings what he thinks fitting. I see what he thinks.
lines.greet_again: You came back, so I was not too dear. Sit. Drink. Tell me who is on the water.
rumour: Three kings share the Franks now, and each fears his brothers more than he fears me. It is a good time to be a guest.
Fleets pass this shore and do not land. Your priests say I am the wolf. Ask the shepherds how many sheep they lost this year.
My brother wants the river town. He will have it. He was always the one who could wait.
lines.saying: A gift looks for a gift. A Frank calls it a toll and writes it down, and then it looks for nothing.
lines.farewell: Go safely along my shore. Past it, you are your own man's worry.

people.source: Historical: Harald 'the Younger', a Danish exile, given Walcheren and the places round it by Lothar I in 841 (Annales Bertiniani 841, which calls him a persecutor of the Christian faith and a worshipper of demons; Nithard iv.2); dead by 850; brother of Rorik (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_the_Younger; Rorik_of_Dorestad). That Danes lived here has left 'no tangible evidence' (kzgw.nl): his hall, his looks and his words are invented. 'A gift looks for a gift' turns Hávamál 46 (the thought, not a translation)

stories.title: The old pennies
stories.summary: The islanders still keep the small thick pennies of their grandfathers in pots and under hearths, and from the harvest of 794 the king's new penny is the only one that passes. Somebody who knows three reckonings can buy dead coin here by weight and make it live again, at a mint or on a Dane's scale.
stories.picture: A brooch-maker's hands tipping a clay pot of small thick silver coins onto a sheepskin by a pit hearth, a merchant's folding scale beside them, firelight.

beats.text: Reginbert has cried the king's order on the street: the new penny in every place and market. A woman holds out a handful of old ones and asks you what she is to do with them.
Wilbraht shows you which of the old pennies are good silver and which are half copper, by the ring and the bite of a file. He will buy them himself for the melt, at a brooch-maker's price.
At the mint in the upper town the moneyer takes old coin by weight less his cut. If he learns you sort before you bring, his cut is less.
On the Danes' strand no stamp counts and the old small pennies still go on the scale with everything else. What is dead coin on Walcheren is silver here.
Wiltrud says who still has a pot under the hearth, if she thinks you paid the last widow fairly.
On the terps of Westergo they still count by the light weight, and an old penny is a penny. Nobody there has heard the king's order cried.

endings.how: You bought the old coin by weight at a fair price and carried it to the mint at Dorestad.
endings.text: The island's dead silver comes back up the river as new pennies. Sigimar begins to take your word on what is in the bag.
endings.reward: A steady small profit each visit until 810; the moneyer's trust (the thread's flag sv_moneyer_trusts, set at Dorestad); Reginbert writes your name in his tally as an honest dealer.

endings.how: You carried the old pennies north and sold them on a Dane's scale at Ripa.
endings.text: Better silver for the islanders than the mint would give, and for you. Wilbraht's friend at Ripa weighs fairly, and you learn the nick and the weights from him.
endings.reward: The best price for old coin; a friend at Ripa; the northern weights (the thread's flag sv_scale, set at Ripa); Wiltrud's good word.

endings.how: You tried to pass old pennies at face in a Frankish market after the order.
endings.text: A toll man upriver turns the coin over, then turns you over to the count's man. The fine is the king's; the story reaches the island before you do.
endings.reward: Nothing gained: a fine (the thread's flag sv_old_coin), and Reginbert cool for a year. Wilbraht finds it funny and gives you a riddle about it.

stories.reward: A trade in old silver nobody else on the Rhine bothers with, and the trust of either the moneyer or the Danes' scale.

stories.title: What stood at the west end
stories.summary: About 796 a learned man far away is writing the life of the bishop who broke the island's idol a hundred years ago, and a monk comes asking the old people what they were told. Two families remember it differently: Bernhild's, who saw a bishop struck and not hurt, and Wilbraht's, whose forefather held the sword.
stories.picture: A weathered oak cross on a bare patch at the end of a street of plank houses, mussel shells at its foot, a monk with a wax tablet talking to an old woman while a young craftsman watches from a doorway.

beats.text: A monk of Echternach is on the strand with a wax tablet. His abbot has asked a great teacher for the saint's life, and the teacher wants to know what is still said where it happened. Nobody will talk to him. He asks you to ask.
Bernhild tells what her grandmother saw: the idol down, the keeper's sword on the bishop's head, no blood, and the keeper dead on the third day. She also says the sword was blunt.

If Wilbraht trusts you he says whose great-grandson he is. In his house the keeper died of shame and a fever, and the bishop's men had wanted to kill him and were stopped. He asks you not to give the monk his name.
At Saint Martin's the bishop's clerks want the island's account for their own house, which was Willibrord's. They pay in wax or in a good word, and ask who told you.
On a feast at the palace the teacher himself may be met. He asks one question: was the man who struck the bishop forgiven? What you answer goes into no book, but he remembers who answered.

endings.how: You gave the monk both tellings and kept Wilbraht's name out of it.
endings.text: The book says what such books say. But the monk has heard that the keeper's kin are baptised and make brooches, and he leaves a blessing at the door of the hearth, which Wilbraht pretends not to notice.
endings.reward: Wilbraht a fast friend (a brooch of his best work each year you call); Echternach's wool from its land by the Scheldt mouth sold to you first; standing with the church at Traiectum.

endings.how: You brought the monk to Bernhild only, or named Wilbraht to him.
endings.text: The monk has his miracle and his witness. If you named Wilbraht, a priest comes at Easter and preaches at the cross about the sons of idol-keepers, and the brooch-maker does not look up when you pass.
endings.reward: The bishop's thanks at Traiectum and a place for the house in the prayers of Saint Martin's; Wilbraht cool or worse if he was named.

endings.how: You told the monk that nobody remembers anything.
endings.text: He goes home with an empty tablet. The mussel shells go on appearing at the foot of the cross. The island decides you are one of its own.
endings.reward: Every islander a little warmer (Wiltrud, Bernhild, Wilbraht); no thanks from any church. Bernhild tells you where the sheep lie before a gale, which is worth more at sea.

stories.reward: A friend for life on one side or the other, and the knowledge of who on the island will keep a secret for you.

stories.title: A week before Saint John's
stories.summary: In 836 Witla and the town on the Scheldt burn, and Count Eggihard and the emperor's Dane Hemming have forty spears and an island without a wall. A week before Saint John's in 837 the fleet comes on the morning tide: the count and the Dane die, women are led away north, and tribute is taken here and at Dorestad.
stories.picture: Dawn on a grey flood tide seen from a high dune: a line of striped sails standing in past white water on the shoals, a boy running down the dune path, the long street still asleep below.

beats.text: Eggihard asks what you saw on the river, and then asks more of you: carry his word to the palace at Noviomagus that the island cannot be held without ships. He has sent it before. A merchant's eyes may count for more than a count's letter.
The palace hears you, courteously. The emperor is bound for Rome this year. Ships have been ordered; they are always being ordered.
Tell the river town what is coming down the coast, and those who believe you put their silver in the ground before the fleet arrives.

Hemming stands on the dune at first light and says they will come on a morning flood with the wind behind them. He is right within the week. Those the watch wakes in time drive their beasts inland over the marsh.
The count and the Dane lie in the fenced graves. Unno says who was taken, and that the Danes' markets are where to look, before winter.

On the Danes' strand a dealer has Frisian women from the west coast. The king of the Danes is said to have had the leaders of the raid killed (?), and to want Frisia for it. Berntrud can be bought back, at a price that goes up when the dealer hears you want one woman and not a lot.

A ring of stacked sods rises by the dunes, a stretch for every house, so that next time there is somewhere to drive a beast and a child. Unno asks any skipper bound north to ask after his sister before winter.

endings.how: You carried the count's word upriver before the fleet came and warned Dorestad.
endings.text: The ships do not come in time; they never could have. But the watch was awake, more of the island's people reached the marsh than would have, and on the river some had buried what they owned before the tribute was named.
endings.reward: The thread's flag df_warned; Unno a fast friend for his lifetime, with salt at the hearth price for the house; a word in your favour at the inquiry at Noviomagus.

endings.how: You went north with silver before winter and bought Berntrud back.
endings.text: She comes home in your boat, saying nothing until the dunes are in sight. Unno takes the salt rake down and gives you the rest of the year's boiling without counting it.
endings.reward: A full cargo of salt, free, and the first of it every autumn after; the deed of buying captives free weighed as a ransom, not a purchase; every door on the strand open to your heirs.

endings.how: You did neither: it was not your island.
endings.text: The Chronicle's voice has it in a line. Unno sells you salt at the price he sells it to anyone. Nobody on the strand asks where you were.
endings.reward: Nothing lost but what might have been: no friend here in the Danish years, when one would be worth a great deal.

stories.reward: Somebody on Walcheren who owes your house more than silver, in the years when the island has a heathen lord.

stories.title: The guest's gift
stories.summary: From 841 the island is Harald's, by the gift of a Christian king, and there is no toll: a guest brings what he thinks fitting and the lord decides whether it was. The fleets pass the strand by, the priests stay away, and a merchant must choose whose peace he trades in.
stories.picture: Inside a long oak hall by firelight: a red-bearded Dane on the high seat with silver on his arms, a Frisian salter setting down sacks before him, a merchant waiting with something wrapped in cloth.

beats.text: No king's man looks in your hull. Two Danes do, without touching anything, and one of them says the lord is at home and likes to meet his guests.

Harald takes no toll. Unno tells you beforehand what was thought fitting last year: wine, a good cloak, never coin, and never a blade, which is death by the emperor's law and an insult besides if it is a poor one.
The bishop's people ask whether it is true that Christians on Walcheren serve a man who worships demons, and whether you sat at his table. They write down the answer.

After the three kings share the realm, the river mouth is a border: the abbey at Ganda is one king's and its wool land by the sea is in another's, under Harald. The cellarer wants his wool carried out, quietly, by someone the Dane lets pass.
Harald is dead and his brother has the river town. A man who was Harald's guest is known to Rorik's toll man before he opens his mouth, for good or ill.

endings.how: You brought a fitting gift each year and sat at Harald's table.
endings.text: On his shore nothing of yours is touched, and his men turn a strange sail away from your boat once, without being asked. Churchmen upriver are cool. When Rorik takes Dorestad his toll man already has your name, and it is a good one.
endings.reward: No search and no toll at Walichrum from 841 to 850 for one gift a year; safe water along the island; a warm word with Rorik's man at Dorestad from 850. Standing with the church at Traiectum falls a little.

endings.how: You never entered the hall: your gift went with the strand's, in Unno's sacks.
endings.text: Harald knows there is a merchant who does not come to see him and lets it be, since the salt is good. The bishop's clerk writes that you kept from the heathen's table. Both things are true.
endings.reward: Trade at Walichrum on the islanders' terms: salt and wool at Unno's price, no favour from Harald and none lost with the church. The cellarer at Ganda trusts you with his wool.

endings.how: You would not trade under a heathen lord, and said so.
endings.text: You are not harmed; you are not welcome. Your boat lies off other strands in these years. The annalist would have approved, and the annalist does not buy salt.
endings.reward: Thanks at Traiectum and a letter of the bishop's good word, of use in any Frankish port; Walichrum shut to the house until Harald is dead.

stories.reward: A known name with the Danes who hold the river mouths, or with the church that detests them: not both.

stories.title: The side room
stories.summary: Bernhild's sister Thiadwih has a sickness that has eaten her face, and has not left the side room of the house in eleven years. Bernhild asks for nothing, but honey, clean linen and a salve from the far coast would be worth more to her than silver, and she pays her debts.
stories.picture: A dim side room of a plank house, a woman seated with her back to us and a linen cloth over her head, her sister kneeling beside her with a bowl; through the open door bright marsh and sheep.

beats.text: You notice Bernhild buys honey and linen she plainly does not use herself. Wiltrud tells you why, and tells you not to say she told you.
A skipper from the east coast says there is a wise woman at Emuthon who makes a salve for sores that will not close. She does not sell it for coin.
The wise woman wants to know who it is for and how long she has had it. She gives the salve for a fleece of marsh wool and a promise, and says it will ease and not mend.
When Thiadwih dies she is laid in the fenced graves like anyone, head to the west, in a coffin of old boat planks. Bernhild asks if the planks may come from a boat of yours.

endings.how: You brought the salve, or honey and linen each time you called, and said nothing about it.
endings.text: Thiadwih lives some years more, easier. You never see her. One day there are two cups set out when you come by the marsh path, and one is carried into the side room.
endings.reward: Bernhild a fast friend: wool and cheese at the price she gives kin, and a share of her flock offered on halves. She tells Unno, who is a child, what house yours is.

endings.how: You gave planks from your own boat for the coffin.
endings.text: A strake of your boat goes into the ground at the fenced graves with a penny on Thiadwih's right shoulder. The islanders bury their own this way and nobody else's.
endings.reward: The island counts the house as kin: lodging free at Wiltrud's, and the right to bury your own dead in the fenced graves. The boat needs a new strake.

endings.text: Bernhild sells you cheese as before. She never mentions a sister, and you do not learn her name.

stories.reward: A household on the marsh that treats the house as kin, and whose grandson is the man who speaks for the strand forty years on.

works.name: A salt hearth on the marsh
works.what: A stretch of salt-soaked ground, a row of clay hearths under a reed roof and a salter working it on halves. The ground is dug, burned and washed, and the brine boiled down in clay pans.
works.needs: The leave of whoever holds the hall (the steward, the count, or Harald for a gift); peat for the fires; a salter you trust, which means Unno or his kin.
works.gives: Each autumn sixteen sacks of salt wait at the hearth for the house. Unfetched, they are sold there at the cheap price and the silver kept for you.
works.picture: A row of low clay hearths under a reed roof on open marsh, white smoke lying flat, a man raking salt, sacks on a sledge.
works.source: works_793.json salt_pan (the shared work, with its cost and yield); salt boiled from salt-soaked soil on Walcheren: kzgw.nl

works.name: Ewes on the marsh, on halves
works.what: Twenty ewes bought into a marsh flock and herded with the shepherd's own, the wool and the cheese shared half and half.
works.needs: A shepherd who will take them: Bernhild, if she counts you a friend, or her kin after her.
works.gives: Each year at the shearing three sacks of raw wool and four wheels of cheese wait for the house.
works.picture: Sheep on green salt marsh with a notch cut in the ear, a woman with a crook counting them through a hurdle gate.
works.source: works_793.json flock_share; sheep farmers on salt marsh: ten Harkel and others 2023

works.name: A fire on the high dune
works.what: An iron basket on an oak post at the top of the tallest dune, peat and a boy to tend it on the nights when ships are looked for. The shore has no tower or stone to steer by.
works.needs: Oak for the post, which must be brought; the leave of the hall; from 834 the count wants it lit only on his word, since a light shows a strand to anyone.
works.gives: Coming in to Walichrum by dusk or in haze, the grounding check on the shoals is easier by one word. Every skipper using the strand knows whose fire it is.
works.picture: A fire basket burning on a post at the top of a dune at dusk, a ship's sail small on a darkening sea, white water to the left.
works.source: works_793.json beacon; de Man 1899 (no tower or stone building); the Banjaard shoals: Research/water_levels/north_sea_core.md. A beacon here is not recorded (?)

works.name: New pales for the fenced graves
works.what: The oak fence round the long grave field is rotting at the foot. New pales, and a new trunk for the west gate, set by the islanders with your timber.
works.needs: Two loads of oak timber landed on the strand; a household on the island that will speak for you (Bernhild or Wiltrud friendly).
works.gives: The house may bury its dead here, and is remembered at the graves. Islanders' feeling rises, and stays risen for your heirs.
works.picture: Men setting fresh pale oak stakes in a long fence beside grey old ones, a gate of two huge trunks behind them, low grave mounds inside.
works.source: de Man 1899 (the grave field at Westhove, fenced with oak pales, 325 paces by 70, with a gate of two great trunks on the west). The repair is invented

works.name: Your stretch of the ring wall
works.what: Twenty paces of the sod rampart, cut, carried and stacked at your cost, and a place inside for your goods when the sails are seen.
works.needs: The year after the raid; diggers hired from the island; the leave of whoever orders the wall, which is nowhere recorded.
works.gives: A store inside the wall that raiders do not reach: goods left at Walichrum are safe in a raid year. Unno's kin keep the key.
works.picture: A curved bank of stacked sods as high as two men with a wet ditch before it, men passing sods hand to hand up a plank.
works.source: works_793.json wall_share; the ring fort: Ufkes 2012 (begun 835-838 on his dating; others later) (?); who built it is unknown

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The island's own boat: mussel and shrimp gatherers work the creeks in them, and the menders can build one from landed oak and old planks.
ships.picture: A small open boat on creek mud with baskets of mussels in her, a man in the water to his knees pushing her off.
ships.source: de Man 1899 (mussel and shrimp shells in the dung heaps); ship_classes_793.json

ships.note: The abbeys of Ganda and Echternach have land round the river mouth and boats to fetch its wool; an old one is sometimes to be had from a cellarer who wants a new one.
ships.picture: A ten-pace sailing boat with six oars drawn up on a strand, sacks of wool being handed aboard, a monk with a tally stick.
ships.source: ten Harkel and others 2023 (the abbeys' land round the Scheldt mouth and the trade in Frisian cloth); the sale is the game's (?)

ships.note: Ships for England wait here for a wind, and some end here: an English clinker ship of oak felled in 769 near Hamwic was broken up on this island. An old sea-going hull, patched, for a house that cannot yet pay for a new one.
ships.picture: A broad clinker-built merchant ship with a tall stem sitting upright on mud at low water, her seams being caulked, her yard lowered.
ships.source: Ufkes 2012 (planks of an English clinker ship in the ring fort); traffic_793.json (three in four long-distance callers here are of this class)

ships.note: Rhine barges bring pots, querns and oak down to the sea and are not always worth towing back. The islanders bury their dead in the planks of them.
ships.picture: A long flat-bottomed barge with a towing mast lying on rollers on a bank, three strakes off, a stack of old planks beside her.
ships.source: ten Harkel and others 2023 (Rhineland oak arriving as barges; a coffin made from a Rhine barge of oak felled after 851)

ships.note: In Harald's years a Danish ship can be bought from a man of his hall who has won a better one. She is not asked about, and the Franks upriver will look hard at her.
ships.picture: A lean Danish ship with a high curved stem and shields off, drawn up among broad Frisian hulls, a Dane sitting on her rail.
ships.source: the grant of 841 (Annales Bertiniani); that Danes lived or sold ships here is not shown by any find (kzgw.nl) (?)

sayings.text: Count the sheep by the legs and divide by four.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: a Frank's joke about how the islanders reckon

sayings.text: The emperor's ships are like the Last Day: promised, certain, and not this year.
sayings.source: invented; the fleet was ordered in 810 and again in 837 (Annales regni Francorum 811; Annales Bertiniani 837)

sayings.text: A Frisian's cloak ends where a Frank's begins to be useful.
sayings.source: invented, after Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (the short Frisian cloaks the emperor would not pay full price for); not a quotation

sayings.text: Stubborn, fickle as the waves, afraid of no law, and taught only by miracles.
sayings.source: what a churchman said of the islanders: Thiofrid of Echternach, about 1103, as given at frisiacoasttrail.blog; our rendering, and a LATER text, so said of them and not by them

sayings.text: Bury a man with a penny on his shoulder, so he can say he has paid.
sayings.source: invented, for a true custom: coins laid on the right shoulder of the dead in the Domburg coffins (de Man 1899)

sayings.text: I have one tooth and bite two cloaks together. I am closed in the morning and open at night. What am I?
sayings.source: invented in the Exeter Book's manner (a riddle with a plain answer: a brooch); not from the Exeter Book

sayings.text: This year the heathen laid waste Walicrum, and led many women away captive.
sayings.source: Annales Xantenses 837 (von Simson 1909), our rendering: the Chronicle voice for the year of the raid

sayings.text: A cup with no foot is an honest host: you cannot put it down until you have finished.
sayings.source: invented; a footless green glass cup was found on the Domburg beach (de Man 1899)

sayings.text: He takes no toll. He takes a gift. The difference is who is thanked.
sayings.source: invented; the gift in kind under Harald is the note in trade_year_793.json

easter_eggs.text: Six hundred years before you, a dealer in pottery who traded with Britain set up a stone here to a goddess, for goods kept safe. It lies under the dune with many others. Nobody alive knows her name, and you will not find it.
easter_eggs.source: the altar of Marcus Secundinius Silvanus, negotiator cretarius Britannicianus, to Nehalennia (livius.org); the shrine was found in January 1647 and lay under the dune until then

easter_eggs.text: A shepherd says his grandfather saw a stone woman in the sand after a great gale, seated, with a dog beside her and a basket in her lap. By spring the sand had her again. He thinks she was somebody's mother.
easter_eggs.source: invented (?): whether anything of the shrine showed before 1647 is not known. The seated goddess with a dog and a basket of apples is livius.org

easter_eggs.text: In one of the grave fields the coffins lie in a star round a man with a sword. Nobody says who he was. They say only that it was done before the bishop came.
easter_eggs.source: de Man 1899 (coffins set in a star round a man with a sword); which field, and the islanders' saying, are ours (?)

easter_eggs.text: A ewe's hoof turns up a gold piece the size of a fingernail, with the name of Dorestad on it. The steward says it is not coin. Wilbraht says it was, when there were kings who could not write.
easter_eggs.source: Metcalf and Op den Velde 2009-10: before 690, gold tremisses of Dorestad are commoner at Domburg than at Dorestad

easter_eggs.text: There is not a horse on the island. Ask why and you are told: what would it eat that a sheep does not eat better?
easter_eggs.source: de Man 1899: bones of cattle, sheep and pig in the dung heaps, and none of horse; the answer is ours

easter_eggs.text: The menders say the tall-stemmed English ship on the bank was built of oak felled near Hamwic in the year the old king of the Franks died. They are a year out.
easter_eggs.source: Ufkes 2012: English ship planks of oak felled 769 near Hamwic; Pippin died in 768

easter_eggs.text: After Easter in the year of the raid a star with a tail stood in the sky for many nights. It comes back about every seventy-six years. Nobody here will see it twice.
easter_eggs.source: Annales Xantenses 837; the comet of 837 was Halley's (frisiacoasttrail.blog)

easter_eggs.text: The annal of the great flood says the sea rose almost to the tops of the dunos. It is the islanders' own word, written by a man who had no Latin for what they live behind.
A woman in the ring wall wears on her breast a silver coin with writing no priest can read, set in fine wire. It was struck in a land of mountains beyond Constantinople, in 866.
easter_eggs.source: de Man 1899: an Abbasid dirham struck in Armenia in 866, set in filigree as a pendant, from the Domburg beach. Shown only from 867

easter_eggs.text: From about 822 the pennies laid on the shoulders of the dead show a temple with a cross, and the words of the Christian faith round it. The dead here are buried with the emperor's creed and in no churchyard.
easter_eggs.source: de Man 1899: temple-type deniers of Louis the Pious in the coffins; the year the type begins is from memory (?)

easter_eggs.text: A small bronze bell hangs at the neck of the ewe that leads Bernhild's flock. It will be found in the sand.
easter_eggs.source: de Man 1899: a small bronze bell among the beach finds; whose it was is ours

unlocks.how: Call three times, pay what you owe, and bring her true news from Lundenwic once.
unlocks.gives: Lodging at Walichrum costs nothing; act:rumours here gives the newest word first; npc alewife feeling +10. Her heir keeps the bench for yours.

unlocks.how: Be a friend of Bernhild's house (the side room), or stand with the island in the year of the raid.
unlocks.gives: act:buy_at_source at the salt hearths at the made price all year, not only after Michaelmas; the first sixteen sacks of each autumn kept for the house.

unlocks.how: Let Wilbraht teach you the ring and the file on the old small pennies (the old pennies).
unlocks.gives: Old and foreign coin is valued true before you buy it; the loss at any mint is less by a part. The game sets flag walichrum_old_coin_eye; act:test_silver succeeds as 'sure'.

unlocks.how: Fund the new pales for the fenced graves, or give planks of your own boat for Thiadwih's coffin.
unlocks.gives: act:bury at Walichrum is open to the house; a merchant or crewman buried here is remembered at act:remember, and the islanders' feeling toward the heir starts at friendly instead of easy.

unlocks.what: The guest of the lord of Walcheren
unlocks.how: Between 841 and 850, bring Harald a fitting gift in person each year (the guest's gift).
unlocks.gives: No search and no toll here in those years; raiders of the Danes leave your boat alone within a day's sail of the island (a guess for the tuning); flag walichrum_haralds_guest, which Rorik's toll man at Dorestad reads from 850.

unlocks.what: The marks of the river mouth
unlocks.how: Take the pilot at the creek strand three times, or sail the mouth three times yourself (unlocks_793.json unlock_pilot_maas).
unlocks.gives: No pilot's fee on this water and the grounding check on the bar passed as 'sure', as the shared unlock says. The pilot met here is cast.gerlef, who wants a pupil.

unlocks.what: A stretch of the ring wall, and a place inside it for the house's goods
unlocks.how: From 838, pay diggers for a full stretch of the ring by the dunes (the card harbour.sods_for_the_ring.walichrum; the work walichrum.work.wall_share).
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_work_walichrum_wall_share: goods left at Walichrum are safe in a raid year; Unno's kin keep the key
